heading: 14 Telling Off the West
title_zh: 第十四章　數落西方
src: Concern over Japan’s foreign relations had helped to shape Uchimura’s career, and, except for the period between his retirement from the Yorozu Chôhô and his participation in the Second Coming Movement, it remained a major interest. As a specialist on foreign affairs in the Yorozu, Uchimura had recommended Western ways to readers. When he again turned his eyes to the world beyond Japan, the self-perception of the Japanese had changed greatly. More self-confident, they no longer considered everything Western to be therefore better. Uchimura agreed; what he saw around him seemed in part to fulfill his earlier dreams. He encouraged deshi to assist the needy in other lands. He enjoyed a wider circle of friends from abroad. And he turned, as a representative of his people, to denounce the attitudes and acts of others who appeared to denigrate Japan. The vigorous use of the English language at first refreshed him but later debilitated him as he discovered that even his fluency could not enlist the approval of foreigners.

The discussion begins with an explanation of how Uchimura’s fellow Japanese understood the word foreigner. They separated the world into categories, domestic and foreign, with the understanding that the word foreign referred to the representatives of Western Europe and America. They could also easily be lumped together under the rubric of white men, though in general they were referred to by the catch-all term gaijin, “those from outside the borders.” Peoples from other parts of the world were referred to by the name of their lands but were not included with gaijin.

When the distinction was seen by Japanese and expressed as racial, “white” against “coloured,” this difference, as in Kanzô’s childhood, continued to reflect economic status. The white peoples seemed infinitely wealthier. Uchimura remembered his earlier painful encounter with these people. When he returned from study abroad, he shunned gaijin, even though his post on the Yorozu Chôhô required him to present the Japanese point of view to foreigners. After he left that job, they largely slipped from his mind. He infrequently met them, and when he did his contact became, like that of his well-educated fellows, largely passive. Books by Western thinkers stimulated him, but he limited his writing in English to personal correspondence and, after 1913, one-paragraph meditations on the first page of each month’s Seisho no Kenkyû.

In the final decade of his life, Uchimura returned to wider contact with people from the West. He seemed to be an internationalist similar to other Japanese trained to deal with foreigners, yet, as the following pages show, several characteristics set him apart from the others: the depth of his understanding and the breadth of his contact with Westerners and his concern for the welfare of Africans and fellow Asians. Very few other Japanese understood how the same factors of economic disparity and lack of respect that so rankled him when he met Westerners also affected those from what would become known as the Third World. He knew that Japan had a duty to protest Western assumptions of superiority and to assist those less fortunate. He fostered brotherly contact and missionary outreach as part of Christian faith. He seldom recognized inconsistency betwen his desire to help others and his starchy reaction to those who approached him with the same motive from elsewhere, but he ensured that aid from his group reached recipients through individuals who demonstrated Christian charity. A discussion of these reactions to peoples less fortunate introduces the more involved examination of relations with Westerners.

Uchimura and his deshi, in common with almost all the other Protestants in Japan, accepted the need to evangelize as an imperative of their faith. They organized groups of students to take the faith to the countryside in the summer, and they formed missionary societies to collect donations for work in China and Africa.

An ad hoc meeting in 1922 established a missionary society. Two succeeding issues of Seisho no Kenkyû contained four-page supplements for evangelism, and subsequent meetings of the society solicited contributions. Uchimura suggested that they start work in China, since he considered Japan and China one in race and culture. In spite of this propinquity, he continued, the Japanese spirit puts Japanese apart from China and closer to England and the United States. Yet the latter send self-sacrificing missionaries to China. As a beginning, Uchimura suggested a gift to the China Inland Mission. This British organization enjoyed a reputation for practical rural work in close affiliation with Chinese colleagues, a kind of service that appealed to Uchimura. The money from his group went to a country physician. Regular correspondence from this English medical missionary described how he used the money to employ Chinese doctors to assist him.

The work of the missionary society in French Equatorial Africa resulted from contacts that Yûshi established in Germany. There he met Albert Schweitzer, the German organist-theologian-philosopher-physicianevangelist. Schweitzer gave up a brilliant career in Germany to establish a missionary hospital in Africa. By the 1920s, Christians throughout the world knew him as one of the principal embodiments of the Christian duty to assist the less fortunate. Yûshi felt flattered to discover that Schweitzer had read How I Became a Christian and admired his father’s work. Through Yûshi’s introduction, the two elderly men corresponded. Uchimura’s missionary society contributed to Schweitzer’s work. The connection was continued after the Second World War when Japanese physicians influenced by Uchimura served in Africa.

Although this work brought the concerns of the rest of the world to the attention of the Uchimura group, his contact with Koreans familiarized him with other Asians, though technically Koreans were not foreign. Japan had taken over Korea in 1910, but Japanese did not consider Koreans brothers. A bureaucratic Japanese elite administered Korea. Occasional Koreans occupied lower posts, but they enjoyed no real authority. In 1919, a terrifying display of Korean passive resistance warned the Japanese how little control they really exercised. Barbaric Japanese attacks on the demonstrators coupled with token gestures of reconciliation only increased Korean animosity.

Uchimura was one of a very small minority of Japanese who understood Korean aspirations and sympathized with Koreans. He refers to them frequently in his diary. A number of Koreans also subscribed to Seisho no Kenkyû, and several attended Uchimura’s Bible lectures before they returned home. Uchimura’s works have been translated into Korean, and Uchimura remains a respected authority on the Bible there.

The cordial relationship started early. Uchimura worked easily and effectively with Koreans because he respected them and elicited respect in return. To Bell, he wrote, “there is no ‘race-question’ between us. From the way by which I was treated by some haughty heartless American and British missionaries, I know somewhat how I must treat so-called ‘inferior’ races.” In a lecture to a group of young Koreans, Uchimura stressed the essential brotherhood of humans that results from shared work toward a common objective such as Christian evangelism. A Korean subscriber to Seisho no Kenkyû tells how he has read all of Uchimura’s writings “six times” and that, when he realizes that Uchimura is a Japanese, “the enemy Japan becomes peaceful and lovable.” I know of no other mutual affection between Japanese and Koreans. With this experience, it is not surprising that Uchimura disliked his government’s policy, believing that the “poor Koreans have lost their country, and nothing can console them for their loss ... Japan has swallowed a Poland by annexing Korea, and she shall never succeed in completely digesting the morsel.” He respected the intense faith and patriotism of the Koreans. When he mentioned nationalism in his lectures, “those who listen with sweating palms are the students from Korea.” One of the students who listened so intently returned home to become the “Korean Gandhi.”

The colonial administrators in Korea did not welcome the prospect of a visit by Uchimura. His friends invited him, but he learned from contacts in the Japanese government that he would not be welcome. There could be no better proof of his effectiveness with Koreans and their respect for him. To Uchimura and the most enlightened of his colleagues, China and Korea, like Africa, represented areas to which Japanese should express feelings of Christian brotherhood. Japan had the money, and at least some Japanese felt the duty to extend such assistance.

But Korea was not the only part of Asia that attracted attention. Rabindranath Tagore, the East Indian poet-philosopher, and Mahatma Gandhi, the national spiritual leader, became household words in Japan. Their India did not elicit charity but respect for an ancient tradition receptive to but not beholden to the West.

Uchimura included Tagore in a list of “new thinkers,” along with the philosophers Rudolf Eucken, Henri Bergson, and Bertrand Russell. In a Christmas talk on the coming of the magi, he referred to the prophecy by some Westerners that Asians can better interpret Christianity than Westerners. When these people say “Asians,” he noted, they do not necessarily mean “Japanese.” “People like Tagore are really representative Asians. Who can say whether the spirit represented by Tagore cannot best interpret Christ?” In lectures in Japan in 1916 and 1924, Tagore discussed an “Asia” infused with Indian spiritual traditions. Uchimura did not mention these visits. One can assume that, like other Japanese intellectual leaders, he would have disagreed with Tagore’s emphasis on Indian values.

For Gandhi, Uchimura expressed unqualified respect, believing that he represented a more direct expression of the claim for human dignity than did Tagore. Gandhi’s nonviolence in particular appealed. Uchimura read of his sentence to six years of imprisonment, to which Gandhi responded that upon release he would continue his nonviolent objection. Here is Gandhi, Uchimura concluded, using Christian methods against a so-called Christian power! His nonviolence expresses a greater nobility than the partisanship and violence of Cromwell and Milton. Uchimura prayed that the Japanese might match Gandhi’s actions to form a strong basis for Asian independence, but he wondered whether Japan could produce a man like Gandhi, who “seems to have been sent by God as the savior of Asia.”

In Tagore and Gandhi, Uchimura recognized voices like his own. They proudly called themselves “Asian,” accepted the standards of the West, made them their own, and then claimed equality with, or even superiority over, Westerners. With these skills, Gandhi would save Asia. No Korean could talk to the Japanese overlords as Gandhi talked to the British, but perhaps, Uchimura could hope, particularly from among his own Korean followers, such a man, inspired by Gandhi, might rise up.

Both the desire to help and the welcome given to Asians fell easily under the rubric of a special “mission” for Japan. Uchimura had pondered Japan’s mission in world history for thirty years, but by the mid-1920s many other Japanese shared his concern. One cannot measure the affection that bound together the victims of Western colonialism in various areas, but it eased the task of Japanese generals a decade later when they sought support with soothing noises about Asian brotherhood and Asia for Asiatics. This discussion has dealt with Uchimura’s attitude to certain foreigners but not gaijin, the only foreigners Japanese considered important before 1945. These Western Europeans and North Americans dominated Japanese concerns as Japanese looked beyond their borders. This preoccupation underlies the following detailed reference to Uchimura’s attitudes.

During his final decade, Uchimura continued and reinforced an earlier pattern. He corresponded regularly with gaijin, but in spite of these contacts, and in common with other educated Japanese, he mistrusted Westerners as a group. His dislike rested on fact. Westerners did not appreciate the niceties of polite Japanese social discourse or the accomplishments of Japanese people. Uchimura founded an English-language magazine to educate them about Japanese virtues. After two years in the attempt, he decided to devote his “remaining energies” to his Japanese-language magazine. Each of these topics merits attention.

Early in the 1920s, Uchimura lost the last among his foreign friends who had introduced him into the faith. Bishop Harris died. Uchimura had remained close to Harris, even though his appointment as bishop first in Japan and then in Korea between 1904 and 1916 left Harris with little leisure time. His accoutrements as bishop would have put off Uchimura, who disliked ecclesiastical authority of any sort. His attitude changed when Harris retired in 1916. He had become a celebrity. Tokutomi Ichirô covered Harris’s retirement in Korea for the English-language newspaper in Seoul. He wrote that Harris’s “six feet of manly form, his crown of silver hair, his heart filled with the joy of heaven and with love for men, his face bright as the dawn, fearing not the devil nor the world, his calm and confident tread, these all explain what sort of man he is.”

Harris’s recognition by official Japan matched his imposing presence. An Imperial decoration in 1898 had commemorated his work among Japanese in California. Another one the year of his retirement undoubtedly reflected official recognition that he, as bishop, had commended Japanese administration of Korea. A few years later he was said to have received more Imperial decorations than any other foreigner. Uchimura did not publicly disagree with his old sensei over his views, although his usually more reserved friend the Presbyterian leader Uemura Masahisa did criticize Harris with the terse comment that Japanese did not need friends who so wrongly praised their country.

The retired bishop was quite different from the widower who had together with Uchimura mourned the death of Mrs. Harris almost a decade earlier. Now Harris became once again the benefactor who had told the young author shortly after its publication how much he had enjoyed Consolations of a Christian. Because of their long mutual appreciation, Uchimura turned to this man when he sought someone to introduce the lecture on Luther that grey day in 1917. Harris, for his part, could introduce with pride Uchimura to the missionaries of Karuizawa and enjoy his presence at receptions in his own Tokyo home.

In January 1921, Harris attended one of Uchimura’s lectures on Romans and himself spoke briefly of his intention, though nearly eighty, to return to preaching. This would not happen. Harris sickened in April and died the following month. In his obituary, Uchimura praised the two Harrises: “They influenced me not by doctrine or church authority but by love and trust.” A few days later Uchimura took to bed with “dizziness, trembling and nausea.” The last intermediary in his own spiritual development had passed on, and Uchimura felt his age.

Two others among Uchimura’s long-standing American friends arrived for visits. Martin Barr, a psychiatrist and friend from Uchimura’s days in Elwyn, Pennsylvania, arrived in April and visited facilities for the care of psychiatric disease during a stay of almost four months. In July, David C. Bell arrived with his son for a visit of nine days. Uchimura introduced them both to his deshi and spent long hours reminiscing with them. The three guests returned home on the same ship, leaving Uchimura marvelling at the warmth of their long correspondence. In Harris and the other Americans, he had enjoyed a depth of friendship uncommon at any age and at wide variance with his attitude toward most gaijin.

In contrast to his close American friends, Uchimura felt the least empathy for the British. In 1922, he wrote to Bell that his single British friend was J.W. Robertson-Scott, whom we have seen escorted by Uchimura to the house of a country landowner. Robertson-Scott had founded the Countryman, a magazine intended for landed gentry and those who aspired to gracious country life. His interest in rural living led him to Japan during the First World War, and The Foundations of Japan, published on his return home, remained the best source on the Japanese countryside until Ronald Dore’s work on land reform forty years later.

When the round of introductions provided for Robertson-Scott brought him to Uchimura, they quickly became friends. Their trip together had given Uchimura a chance to tell Robertson-Scott that the patient, hard-working farmers had been terribly hurt by Japan’s forced modernization. RobertsonScott, returning from the visit, summarized his reaction with a description of Uchimura borrowed from Japanese friends: the “Japanese Carlyle” and “troubler of Israel.” Uchimura saw his friend as an “open rationalist, a strong, honest man.”

If Uchimura felt that he lacked many Anglo-Saxon friends, he had many more in northern Europe. The translations of How I Became a Christian gained him recognition from intellectuals interested in religion. He corresponded with many of them, and Japanese students like Yûshi enjoyed warm welcomes because of his father’s fame.

Uchimura owed many of these contacts to Wilhelm Gundert, whose original translation of How I Became a Christian had sold between 40,000 and 50,000 copies and had led to the other translations. Although they no longer worked together, the Uchimuras and the Gunderts remained friends, and Uchimura told his deshi in 1920 that he and his family had been informed by Gundert “of the beautiful side of the German people.”

Gundert introduced a professor from Tübingen to one of Uchimura’s meetings and interpreted the guest’s remarks into flowing Japanese. Letters to Uchimura from deshi in Europe revealed completely unexpected support there. One wrote from Paris that he had given copies of Representative Men of Japan to the president of the Sorbonne, who had called it a famous classic, and to the statesman Clemenceau, who is reported to have said that if his health permitted he would like to go to Japan to meet the author. On another day, the postman brought a letter from the publisher of Albert Schweitzer who had read Uchimura’s Alone with God and Me, a collection of English-language meditations, and found reading it “like listening to Bach.”

While his writings brought Uchimura into contact with some of the most exciting European scholars of his generation, he was constantly reminded by the missionaries around him that not all foreigners were supermen. As a group, the missionaries seem fated, almost as much because of Uchimura’s prickly personality as anything they did, to suffer unpleasant encounters with Uchimura. He remained critical and quick to infer condescension from their words.

Missionaries and his followers thought that Uchimura was in some way “antimissionary.” In fact, numerous references to the problem so far indicate that his reaction was not simple. He accepted invitations to stay in the homes of missionaries. Their hospitality qualified them as what became known among Japanese pastors as “good missionaries,” those who followed normal decencies of social intercourse and shared vocation. Those who were not “good missionaries” were not known as “bad missionaries.” “Bad missionaries” formed the basis of the stereotypes. A look at these preconceptions reflects the specific nature of his relations with missionaries as Uchimura aged.

His general case against missionaries rested on three points: they do not respect us or our culture; they do not learn our language; and they put church and expediency above faith. Because missionaries do not respect our culture, they consider us all like our most feckless few. After a Sunday lecture, a member of the audience seeks an appointment with Uchimura and requests money. The attempt spoils Uchimura’s day. “I imagined someone waiting for a missionary to come down from his pulpit and entreating the missionary for money. It made me feel miserable,” presumably because the missionary would thereby conclude that all Japanese sought handouts from gullible foreigners. When a missionary visited Uchimura and asked on whom he depended, Uchimura said, “God, myself and my countrymen.” The missionary asked how such faith could be developed in Orientals, in apparent disbelief that any convert could evangelize without assistance from missionaries. Uchimura thought that such a comment displayed ignorance of Japanese culture.

This ignorance was demonstrated, he believed, by the little effort that missionaries put into work in the Japanese language. In one of his short English-language meditations entitled “Missionaries and Language,” he noted succinctly that

> We know of English and American missionaries who stayed in Japan twenty, or thirty, or forty years, who yet are not able to speak respectable Japanese ... As to the reading capacity of missionaries, it is next to nothing. Not one among a hundred can read vernacular newspapers, and we know of no one who can read ordinary Japanese literature in the original. No wonder that they cannot understand us, and that after spending half their lifetime in this country, they still remain utter strangers to us. The fact that these missionaries despise our language is a sure evidence that they have no true love for our souls.

His final point derives from the first two: individuals who show so little empathy for Japanese put the expansion of their own denomination above the faith itself. Paul attempted to minimize cultural differences between himself and others, but missionaries to Japan differ. They go so far as to ask us to change our religion, to give up our customs, to fight with our relatives: yet they themselves cannot change their denominations. And they judge their work by the numbers of their converts.

That these sketches are overdrawn but otherwise well founded is demonstrated by Uchimura’s activities in the summer of 1926. Uchimura rented a Japanese-style house a few miles west of Karuizawa in the mountains west of Tokyo. There he had lectured with great success in 1918. Karuizawa had been developed as a refuge from summer heat by members of the missionary community. For a few months each summer, it was probably the most international community in Japan. His diary tells us that during this period Uchimura went into Karuizawa five times as a break from the continued reading and writing that characterized his “vacation.”

On one occasion, he visited his old friend Hannah Riddell (1855-1932), an Anglican missionary whom he calls “a humble and wise woman,” the “mother” to the 200,000 lepers in Japan. He thanks God that he can contribute to her work. Miss Riddell has “followed the example of Florence Nightingale.” Her work begun in 1895 among the lepers of Kyushu “has won a lasting place for her in the annals of social welfare in Japan.”

Three days later, at the request of the Canadian Methodist missionary Daniel Norman (1864-1941), the father of the historian Herbert Norman, Uchimura lectured at the “church for Japanese” in Karuizawa. He told his audience of well over 200 the story of William S. Clark and concluded that the lay foreigners hired by the government had proved better evangelists than the missionaries. If missionaries should leave Japan, Christianity would still flourish. Uchimura later told his diary that he regretted his words when he had been invited by a missionary to speak but thought he had to describe things as they were.

Later he hired a taxi to show the family the sights of Karuizawa, the “summer capital for missionaries and Tokyoites,” with the conclusion that to “see it one time with the family is plenty.” Less than a week later a memorial service for the third anniversary of the Great Earthquake took him back to Karuizawa. There a British missionary on the street enraged him by treating him “as a child ... We Japanese believers should cooperate and send such missionaries away as soon as possible. As long as they are here, Christ’s holy name will only be sullied.”

A week later the American Merrell Vories invited Uchimura to his home. Early in the twentieth century, Vories had given up his architectural practice in the United States to evangelize the Japanese when doctors predicted that his tuberculosis gave him a year to live. His health restored in Japan, he married a Japanese woman, opened an architectural office, and used the profits from the Japanese sale of the American medicinal ointment Mentholatum as well as Hammond organs to establish a Christian cooperative brotherhood. Uchimura praised the work of Vories and urged his readers to remember that such Americans existed. A third of a century after Uchimura’s death, Vories quickly produced correspondence from Uchimura in response to questions about his relations with him.

When he visited Vories, Uchimura heard that many gaijin were abandoning Christianity in favour of Buddhism, so that Japanese must espouse Christian principles to gaijin, as he had stated a few months earlier. Such being the case, “I cannot understand the intent of missionaries who try to teach Christianity to us while not realizing that it languishes in their home lands.”

These five short visits to Karuizawa demonstrate various aspects of the problems that followed Uchimura’s attempt to work with missionaries. Numerous sources confirm that Hannah Riddell, Merrell Vories, and Daniel Norman were “good” missionaries. Yet the Karuizawa resort had separate churches for Westerners and Japanese. The “church for Japanese” where Norman had held his meeting made one wonder about vaunted Christian brotherhood. Uchimura himself fretted as he said things he thought missionaries disliked to hear. And the British missionary on the street, whatever he did or said, did not disprove stereotypes.

The confusion about missionaries and their role that these examples reflect disfigured Uchimura’s remaining days. Uchimura knew little about why missionaries came to Japan. They volunteered for service in the far corners of the world in response to what they considered a God-ordained imperative. Only a century later are the origins and dynamics of the Protestant missionary movement receiving the attention from historians that they deserve. Coupled with the conviction that they should evangelize in God’s name, missionaries also sought adventure. They informed their supporters about exotic foreign lands when no films, radio, television, e-mail, or Internet provided information. In the “foreign fields,” to use their term, they laboured long and lonely. Summer watering spots like Karuizawa provided their children with a touch of life similar to that “at home,” the countries from which their parents had come. Some missionaries said wryly that missionaries were like manure: spread out in small dollops beneficial but in a group smelly. What made “the social atmosphere of Karuizawa ... not at all congenial” to Uchimura resulted in part from this abnormal concentration of what discounted the mission enterprise in his eyes.

The relations between missionaries and their professional colleagues in the lands to which they went require further study. Such research should also illuminate the latter-day missionary endeavours of government-dispatched technical advisors to less advanced countries. What Uchimura said provides eloquent testimony to the attitudes of a sensitive and proud man who had spent his life in the attempt to gain recognition for his nation’s virtues, but it is only one facet of the story, a facet seldom expressed so clearly. Part of what exercised Uchimura as he visited Karuizawa resulted from two enterprises that had occupied his attention for the preceding two years. In 1924, he joined the Japanese movement in vigorous protest against the new US Immigration Act that proscribed immigration from Asia. Then, early in 1926, he founded an English-language magazine, with missionaries an important part of its intended audience. The two enterprises shaped his final attitudes toward gaijin.

The Immigration Act of 1924 reflected a change in American attitudes toward Japan and caused consternation in Japan itself. Japan had enjoyed high regard in the West ever since its decisive victory in the war against Russia two decades earlier. Japan’s Twenty-One Demands presented to China in the First World War and military intervention in Russia a few years later squandered this goodwill. Opposition to immigrant labour had made Japan a domestic issue in West Coast American politics. Immigrants from other parts of the world posed problems that required immediate action. President Calvin Coolidge had much more on his mind than Japan as he pondered legislation that included a prohibition of immigration from all parts of Asia.

Japanese saw the problem as more simple. They wondered whether they would continue to enjoy the preference among Westerners conferred upon them by their rapid modernization. Japan’s high status in the League of Nations confirmed this special role. Its leaders had named Uchimura’s close friend Nitobe Inazô as an undersecretary general; as such, Nitobe was the only non-European in the inner council of the League. More than seven decades after his retirement passed before another Japanese achieved a similarly high position in an international organization. Nitobe’s initiatives in Geneva would have far-reaching consequences. No one could predict them at the time. Instead, Japanese clung to the expectation that President Coolidge would veto the bill once it had meandered through the committees and houses of Congress. After long consideration of possible consequences, Coolidge signed it and so shattered the hopes of the Japanese. Uchimura wrote that his act might portend “the destruction of Japan.”

Aware that his response might be nothing more than another outbreak of his “patriotic disease,” Uchimura rose to the attack. Newspaper reporters came to him for statements on the assumption that as a Christian he would support the American decision. They were wrong. During the succeeding months, he published thirty-two articles that refer to the act. Most of them appeared in leading secular publications such as the Yorozu Chôhô, where Uchimura had worked twenty-five years earlier. Others came out in the Kokumin Shimbun, which had, with its publication of his acerbic “Observations on the Times,” introduced Uchimura to the secular reading public almost three decades earlier. His reappearance in Tokutomi Sohô’s magazine marked a rapprochement with its founder after they had gone their separate ways for many years. Uchimura now found himself in “complete agreement” with Tokutomi.

In addition to writing his articles, Uchimura sat through long committee meetings with the theologian and Presbyterian Church leader Uemura Masahisa and Kozaki Hiromichi, leader of the Congregationalists. Kozaki had unwittingly started the controversy that drove Uchimura from the YMCA. Uchimura seems to have met Kagawa Toyohiko for the first time on this committee, but he had already known the other two since they posed together for a group portrait at the meeting of young Christian leaders in 1883. Now their mutual concern for their faith and nation overcame dogmatic differences. This cooperation ended before Uchimura left Tokyo for the summer. When he resumed his regular fall schedule, he accepted the Japanese estrangement from the United States as unwelcome fact.

The first articles and speeches bristled with indignation that the United States had broken its 1854 treaty with Japan that proclaimed “permanent friendship.” They then encouraged Japanese Christians to overcome feelings of dependence on the United States. They could do so in practical ways by refusing financial aid and sending missionaries home. Uchimura also urged all Japanese to lower their expectations. They should make more of their resources such as the sea, and they should emulate the peoples of small countries such as Holland and the Jews, who, though few, had profoundly influenced world history. Finally, Japanese should fulfill their mission to provide “true faith” to the world. Their Shinto and Buddhist traditions make them, like the Jews, capable religious leaders. In sum, Japan should forgo material gain in favour of the spiritual traditions that set it apart in the world.

All this activity returned Uchimura to the centre of controversy. The American action opened up once again the issue of basic loyalty: could a Christian be a good Japanese? Uchimura and his Christian colleagues knew very well the problems that this question involved.

The secular press, Uchimura continued, reflected the popular belief that Christians depended on foreign aid and encouragement. Christians should declare themselves on this issue. He recognized that most of those who called themselves “Christians” were “America worshippers.” He had to inform everyone how clearly he differed from this stereotype and put up the following bilingual poster outside his Imaikan:

> Indignation over American Injustice and Unfaithfullness!! Not a sen of American money in this Christian house of worship Uchimura Bible-Study Association. Beikoku no fuji, fushin o okorimasu. Kono Kirisutokyô no kôdô ni wa Beikokujin no kane wa issen ichirin mo tsukaihatte arimasen.
As Uchimura worked with church leaders on their joint statement, he was surprised that the staid Presbyterian Uemura felt even more strongly on the issue.

For most Japanese, the call to lower material ambition implied a rejection of earlier ambition. Educated Japanese would not accept this; most of them did not concern themselves over the spiritual ascendancy that Uchimura advocated to counterbalance lowered material expectations. Although his suggestions elicited little response, his reappearance at the centre of controversy emphasized his identification with national Japanese aspirations. No longer could anyone doubt his loyalty to Japan.

One of the most influential deshi and Japan’s greatest specialist on US politics, Takagi Yasaka, disagreed with Uchimura’s ideas on the act but even more with his cooperation with church leaders on the declaration. Uchimura could consider the leading churchmen’s acceptance of him a recognition of his ideas, but his deshi Takagi reacted differently. He felt his own identity bound up with Uchimura’s criticism of the church, and Uchimura’s cooperation with church leaders seemed to belie his ideals. This apparent contradiction would increasingly bother Uchimura.

As he considered his response to the act, he first decided to address gaijin directly. At sixty-five, he started an English-language monthly magazine with the hope that better knowledge of Japan would persuade Westerners to accept Japanese aspirations. He decided to collaborate with Yamagata Isoh because of Yamagata’s renowned ability to present a persuasive Japanese point of view to Westerners. The new magazine was the Japan Christian Intelligencer. It came out in twentyfour monthly installments beginning in March 1926, almost two years after Coolidge’s act. Its brown cover and forty-four pages fifteen by twenty-three centimetres made it appear a serious journal of opinion, which the contents corroborated. At fifty sen a copy, or five yen a year, it cost two-thirds more than Seisho no Kenkyû and was not cheap, the price reflecting perhaps both the high costs of production and the assumed ability to pay of those whom it addressed. At the end of the first year, the collaboration between Yamagata and Uchimura ceased. Uchimura took over sole direction and changed the format. Until the change, the Japan Christian Intelligencer contained material of a general nature, but under Uchimura alone it emphasized his ideas. Before we look at these contents, it is necessary to see what the two editors anticipated as they started.

In various references, Uchimura listed three motives. First, gaijin in fact understood Japan very little. Even otherwise good friends of Japan made many mistakes: the editor of the Sunday School Times who had led Uchimura to the Second Coming Movement was one. “My patience is gone about his careless way of writing about things Japanese ... He is misleading his country men into great errors, and the effect will be disastrous when the errors are found out by the public.” Second, Buddhists now had their own mouthpiece, the Young East, a monthly started in 1924 with contributions from authorities such as Suzuki Daisetsu(tz) (1870-1966) and Anesaki Masaharu. They, along with Suzuki’s wife, Beatrice, were the best-known authorities who wrote in English on Japanese Buddhism. The Young East was, Uchimura believed, backed by the Buddhist establishment and the Japanese government and sent “free” to world leaders. “I could not bear to see that done, without attempting to show the outside world that Buddhism is not the only religion of Japanese, that Christianity with ... fewer adherents is just as powerful in Japan, if not more so.” Third, and perhaps most important, Uchimura could not look idly on as Christianity died in the so-called Christian countries. “Thus I will put out all my energy as the last act of my life to preach the deep gospel of the son of God simply to the whole world, using the English I have previously learned while in Japan.”

Yamagata Isoh described his motives to start the magazine in the first issue. Throughout his career, he had used the English he had learned under the Scot James Murdoch, with whom he later collaborated on the threevolume History of Japan. Yamagata noted that he had lived so comfortably off royalties from his Japanese-language articles while neglecting his studies and ridiculing his professors that Tokyo Imperial University had expelled him. Kuroiwa Ruiko then hired him for the Yorozu Chôhô, with the reasoning that one sharp enough to get expelled from university “might make a good journalist.” Yamagata then rose to become the editor of the Yorozu and moved in 1909 to fourteen years with the English-language Seoul Press. During that time, he trebled the paper’s circulation and joined the Japanese delegation to the Washington Arms Limitation Conference of 1921-22. He had great experience at improving relations between Japan and the West, and in the Japan Christian Intelligencer he would achieve “his long-cherished ambition” to address gaijin directly.

Yamagata also esteemed Uchimura and his ideals. But for Uchimura’s help that had begun on the Yorozu Chôhô, he “would now be spending his days in prison or more probably would have died on the gallows a long time ago.” After Uchimura left the Yorozu, Yamagata had served as one of his windows onto the world of professional journalism. Yamagata’s son remembers how the friendship included elements of personal belief. One month after the Great Earthquake of 1923, his father, normally bluff and hearty, returned home subdued from a conversation with Uchimura. As he walked into the house, he reported to his wife that, “in fact, it does seem to have been heavenly retribution.” Now, three years later, Yamagata desired as a Christian along with his mentor “to render humanity whatever little service he can as his meanest soldier and most thankful servant.”

The formal party at the tiny Kanda office to introduce the publication drew twenty-five editors experienced in Japan’s English-language press. Their profession had at that time existed for a generation. Almost eight decades later, it would continue much expanded as Japan pours out popular Englishlanguage publications to inform foreigners about Japan.

When the first issue appeared, Uchimura enthused that for “an old man to put out a new magazine is as much fun as the birth of a grandchild.” The magazine itself appeared healthy, containing advertisements from bookstores, the Lion toothpaste corporation, the Mitsubishi Bank, the Misukoshi Department Store, and firms that specialized in Japanese herbal remedies.

As Ota Yûzô points out, one who compares the contents with Uchimura’s earlier English-language secular journalism discovers a different emphasis. In the Yorozu Chôhô, he had advocated the Westernization of Japan and attacked native values. Now he presented Japan as at least the equal if not the superior of the West, proclaiming “Japan’s own special Christianity” and introducing “the best of Japan.” Content aimed at introducing Japanese virtues predominated at first, and Uchimura’s attitudes about Japanese Christianity appeared in greater detail after Uchimura assumed complete responsibility. Discussion of the secular themes therefore precedes those of religion.

The general articles about Japanese life included miscellany on topics that it was assumed interested Westerners, such as the Japanese typewriter, Japanese goldfish, the chesslike game of shôgi, and professions open to women. Others spoke to more sophisticated tastes. Masamune Hakuchô, an important essayist, commended Uchimura’s style as “simple yet full of vigor and force” in an article about the “Christian Influence on Japanese Literature.” A series of short biographies introduced Westerners who had been particularly interested in Japan. They included Philipp Franz von Siebold, the German physician to the Dutch settlement in Nagasaki during the nineteenth century, the historian of Japan James Murdoch, and the German philosopher Rudolph Eucken. Yamagata compared his teacher Murdoch to Lafcadio Hearn: “In their eyes we are no longer inferior people with only skin-deep civilization.” Uchimura called Eucken, “like all truly great men ... great in treatment of common themes ... On reading [Henri] Bergson we felt we had become cleverer men; but after perusing Eucken, we felt we became better men and better Christians.”

Although these individual Western leaders were praised, in general the Japan Christian Intelligencer criticized more than it commended. Yamagata explained the influence of Japanese woodblock prints on Europe in these words: “The old color-prints with their gorgeous coloring and with their striking and audacious designs, appeal to those who are not as yet much advanced in their esthetic culture. That is the reason why they are so much beloved by foreigners to-day and why formerly they were given to countryfolk and children as souvenirs of Yedo. Time will certainly come when foreigners will begin to appreciate works” of the great Japanese painters such as Sesshu. Uchimura dealt no less harshly with Western civilization. “Already this civilization, the Western ‘Christian civilization,’ made havoc of our humble Oriental homes, stamped out our homely virtues, and made us very much like the savages themselves, who think it very philosophical to kill others that they themselves may live and prosper, to exclude other races by color distinctions, and to claim the whole earth as their rightful possession.”

James Murdoch reported at length from Australia on a three-hour interview with the prime minister, William Hughes, who was generally considered anti-Japanese. Hughes demonstrated “a wonderfully high respect for the Japanese ... But naturally he fights shy of having a repetition of the California embroglio in Australia ... Things like the Twenty-one Demands [which had attempted during the First World War to secure control over much of China] made Japan profoundly distrusted.”

A deshi of Uchimura in California added to the generally unsavoury picture of the United States with his report of how rural Americans robbed local Japanese farmers knowing that the law forbids them to own guns. The farmers, defenceless and isolated, become easy prey, particularly when at harvest they had with them the payments for a whole year’s crop.

While introducing such evidence of the clear injustice worked by California laws on Japanese workers, Uchimura stated his own case against the United States through a tongue-in-cheek “Open Letter to Uncle Sam.” After assuring his uncle of his love, Uchimura expresses his dislike of the uncle’s condescending tone, unpredictable reactions, and injustices based on race. When the Japanese state their case, you, uncle, “go on teaching and teaching, scolding sometimes, and ever retaining your patronizing tone. You may not like this my way of writing to you; but you compel me; we on this side of the ocean are being estranged from you more and more.” After stating that he has much more to write but will forbear, Uchimura closes with “Sincerely your ‘rude’ nephew, The Editor of the J.C.I.”

Uchimura found a ready ally in the respected William Elliot Griffis, an American who in early Meiji had taught in provincial Japan and gone on to become one of the most knowledgeable publicists on matters Japanese. Griffis, in an address to the Tokyo America-Japan Society, said, “I hang my head with shame when I think of what my country did in passing a law keeping you out because some of our politicians are afraid of you.” Later in another article, Griffis expressed his support for Uchimura’s independent Christianity.

Here were themes that would continue for many years in the Englishlanguage journalism of Japan. Perhaps the articles on Westerners were the best crafted and provided the greatest information to the Western reader. The attacks on the United Sates expressed very clearly what many Japanese appear to have thought.

Yamagata decided at this point to resign. As a result, in early February 1927, Uchimura rose from his sickbed, donned traditional Japanese garb, and accompanied by Saitô went to the tiny Japan Christian Intelligencer office. There, in a five-minute ceremony, he took over complete control of the magazine. It had not prospered as either editor had hoped. The strategies to attain support from foreign firms had not borne fruit. Advertisements from Japanese companies had all but disappeared. And the circulation, at first 2,000, had fallen to less than 900. In sole control, Uchimura amalgamated offices with his other publications, slashed the price from fifty to twenty sen per copy, and cut the size to twenty-four pages. Sole responsibility rested with him and Suzuki Toshirô, the deshi who would later edit the first and second editions of Uchimura’s complete works. Together they turned to “speak as little as possible about this world and its doings, and as much as possible about the other world and its claims and blessings.” Uchimura’s own concern for religious ideas formed the core of the content. Most impressive were the meditations that dealt with elements of Uchimura’s belief:

> Faith and Thinking Faith is not thinking; what a man thinks is not his faith. Faith is rather being; what a man is is his faith. Thinking is only a part of being; rather a superficial part ... The modern man thinks he can know God’s truth by thinking ... [but] Faith is the soul in passive activity. It is the soul letting itself to be acted upon by the mighty power of God. Passive though faith is, it is intensely active because of the power that works in it. This is the paradox of faith ... The Christian ... is a newly created soul which engenders special activity called faith. Faith is thus a Christian activity of far higher order than thinking. It is the whole soul in beneficent action.

Or on the Apostles’ Creed: “It is not mine because it is the Apostles’, but because it expresses my own belief ... the best possible expression of my faith ... a concise statement of my inner experience.” Or on God: “You ask for proof of his existence? I know of no such proof as will satisfy dry intellect. The proof, if there is one, is experimental, and not theoretical. God, the source [of] life, proves His existence, by giving more life to them who desire to live by Him.” Or on Christ:

> I find in me something which no friendship, not even divine friendship, can take away. That something I feel as a spiritual malady, ineradicable by human means. I was taught to call it SIN, and I might as well call it by that name as any other name ... I found the practical solution of my problem ... in the atoning death of the son of God ... Thus, Christ is my God-saviour. No man could have performed in me this radical change of my being which I experienced when I looked at Christ crucified by faith. To me it was a miracle ... which I call my conversion.”

Or on liturgy: “To me, forms are not only not helps for worship, but positive hinderances ... I worship God inwardly in spirit and serve him outwardly in ordinary human conduct. [This formless Christianity is called] mukyôkai-shugi-no-Kirisutokyo, Christianity of no-church principle ... It is not a negative faith but positive; else my countrymen would never have received it.”

These short passages in company with those that came out monthly in Seisho no Kenkyû provide some of the most relaxed yet comprehensive statements of Uchimura’s ideas. The short comment on mukyôkai, with its deemphasis of liturgy and emphasis on the inward light as expressed in action, explains the core of his belief in fewer words than any other passage.

In addition to his own beliefs, Uchimura introduced native Japanese religions: “Shintoism in its pure form is Piety itself.” Or, again, it “is the simplest possible religion; and the true Japanese brought up under its influence is naturally attracted by the religion which had its beginnings in the worship of Jehovah who had ‘voice and no forms.’” As Shinto shares elements with Christianity, so does Buddhism. People often set them apart, so that belief in one seems to negate the other, but this has not been my experience. Both are profoundly pacifistic, and “all other differences amount to nothing when compared to agreement on this cardinal truth.” Warlike Westerners adopted Christianity and suppressed its essential pacifism. “Christianity an enemy of Buddhism? Not so! Christianity is a sworn enemy of these warlike Westerners, and not of Buddha and his peace-loving disciples. To make Christianity represent the Warlike West, and make it an enemy of Buddhism, a religion of love and non-resistance, is the greatest possible misrepresentation that can be made of it.” These statements about his own belief and elements of other beliefs in Japan would perhaps not have found agreement in many quarters, but they expressed a settled point of view in conciliatory language.

Other essays seemed to demand response, none more so than those that dealt with missionaries or the policies of the countries that sent them. In response to one reader who found his English “shocking,” the editor replied that much more shocking things go on in the United States. They include the fundamentalist preacher in Fort Worth who shot a man in his own church, got out on bail the following day to address 6,000 people, and then received an invitation to speak in New York. “Bad as Japan is, it is not so bad as America is.”

The Japanese language of missionaries in Japan is no less shocking: “When honorific titles are promiscuously applied to men and women of all ranks, and a missionary calls his own wife okusan, an honorable lady, and his parishioner’s wife gusai, foolish woman, no wonder he is often accused of his thoughtless vulgarity. Never was a precious tiding conveyed in more awkward vehicles, and no wonder that a nation was not converted in a day.” Uchimura also laments through a deshi, Tsukamoto Toraji, the tendency of Japanese, under the influence of missionaries, to feel that they must ape Westerners to be Christian. Look at Japanese women in mission schools to see the results of this. “Those Japanese Christians are no more Japanese in their thoughts, moral ideas, manners, and their language even; they are half-Americans. They look neither like men, nor like women, but they are, so to speak, hermaphrodites! For they have lost their meekness ... They have begun, following American female missionaries, to bob, to crop their glossy black hair, which is the special gift of God to adorn them.” In this way, the rational exposition of his ideas became, when he looked at missionaries, less temperate.

One of them, the scholarly Ernest W. Clement, asks, “why it is necessary for you to drag in bitter criticisms or severe attacks upon missionaries or Americans in your writings. I do not mean to imply they are above criticism; I only wonder whether such criticism does not weaken the force of your general argument. It is so strong as to suggest an obsession or a prejudice.” Uchimura did not answer directly, but Clement’s two subsequent contributions to the Japan Christian Intelligencer made Clement, after a certain E.B. Craig, the most published foreigner. His soft-spoken remonstrance seems to have earned him a respectful response.

Not so fortunate were two other Americans who commented on Uchimura’s articles, both apparently in the spirit of well-meant criticism. A veteran missionary with the YMCA drew a scornful reply when he called Uchimura a “spiritual descendant of Continental pietism as it manifests itself in Germany and Scandinavia.” And a venerable lady missionary, H. Frances Parmalee, found herself embroiled in an acrimonious and confused correspondence. An examination of the heated verbal encounter shows how the spectre of bossy Western women continued to perplex Uchimura. Parmalee (1852-1933) was a Congregational missionary teacher who first went to Japan in 1877. She retired in 1924 to the city where Merrell Vories lived. Her letters to the mission headquarters depict her as a “‘typical’ single missionary lady,” with a bent for “informing her superiors about Japanese opinion.” She was a member of the Women’s Christian Temperance Union and had experienced a bout with tuberculosis.

While a guest in a friend’s home, Parmalee read an article in the Japan Christian Intelligencer by Uchimura on sectarianism. It pled the cause of the Japanese convert forced to choose from among the many competing English and American denominations and concluded that “sectarianism is opposed to the very spirit of Christianity.” It ended with the hope that it might “never be transplanted to the virgin soil of the East!”

Returned home, Parmalee sent Uchimura a note. It described the recent movements for church union in Canada and the United States that were consolidating many divergent groups. His statements about the huge numbers of sects were therefore not true, “though they were true fifty years ago.” She then added, “I also think you yourself are making a new sect. It may be called the ‘Uchimura Church,’ one of whose tenets is dislike of other churches.”

Uchimura reacted in a condescending note in romanized Japanese that said her words demonstrated that Parmalee was not his friend (“tomodachi de nai koto ga yoku wakarimashita”), for which reason he would not reply (“watakushi wa go-henji wo sashiagemasen”) except in a public debate in one of his publications (“zasshi no uede ôyake ni”). When she answered with another personal note in English, he responded in the same language, calling her a “coward” for not writing “an open letter to be publicly answered,” and ended with the taunt “why don’t you become a heroine and come forward, and fight with me in public?”

For the succeeding three days, Uchimura wrote to her every day, informing her, among other things, that “American women are much the most unwomanly women in the world, that they as missionaries did much, very much, to destroy the womanhood of China and Japan,” and that with a public answer addressed to Seisho no Kenkyû and the Japan Christian Intelligencer she could “discredit” him and his “works” to their readers “scattered all over the world.” Five days later, he had worked himself into a frenzy: “I think you proud American women are not to be put to silence by one whom you hypocritically call your friend, but despise from the bottom of your heart.” In the same letter, he mentioned an English-language article prepared for publication in the next Intelligencer and told Parmalee that he would send her a copy. It complained that she had judged him “sweepingly by reading only one copy of my magazine” and said that she “must not treat Japanese Christians, especially those of my age, as she would treat school children ... in her familiar, ‘school-ma’am’ style.”

Parmalee replied, “Following the Biblical admonition in Matthew hoping simply to correct the ideas that seemed to me mistaken, I wrote to you privately about what seemed to me a fault.” Uchimura responded with another call to her to reply publicly and in Japanese. He also requested the conciliation of Kimura Seimatsu, who knew both of them and had worked with Uchimura in the Second Coming Movement. Kimura wrote to Parmalee that “Mr. Kanzô Uchimura is full of indignation toward you ... What is the matter? Write me at once.” In her reply, she presented her side of this “most astonishing thing,” wondering why Uchimura had “flared up” and asked “all those questions having no relation to the subject.” She ended with a request that Kimura be “umpire. I thank you for writing me; it seems needless to me that he should make such a great matter of my little effort to have him look at present day sects in a different light.” The following day, having heard that Uchimura had discussed their correspondence before an audience of 700, she sent a second letter to Kimura, who may have relayed its contents to Uchimura.

A few days later Uchimura wrote to Kimura that he would follow Kimura’s suggestions and not distribute the “printed sheet,” by which he probably meant the article that he had prepared for the Japan Christian Intelligencer but had not, contrary to his earlier intention, published. A relieved Kimura informed Parmalee. “It is unfortunate for you. You did not know who Uchimura is? Now you know, don’t you? ... He wrote to me such a good letter today.”

A cynic might easily dismiss this episode as the normal effluent of religious misunderstanding, given a particular redolence by the aging Uchimura’s distemper. Such a dismissal would miss the importance of the exchange. The dialogue, like so much else of Uchimura’s prose, involves a reader in his concerns. The great historian of Japanese thought, Takeda Kiyoko, finds herself getting “worked up” as she reads the letters. Ota Yuzo concludes as he analyzes her article that she has unrestrained admiration for Uchimura’s position, though Ota considers it an example of “Uchimura’s most hateful aspect.” One can only conclude that the event meant more to the participants and means more to later historians than much religious controversy. To understand Uchimura’s position requires more detail.

Uchimura and Parmalee each felt a Christian duty to correct the other, a conviction that grew as the debate continued. Parmalee never realized that Uchimura had met her a third of a century earlier. No longer a struggling young author, he could now talk with the freedom that experience and fame confer. Uchimura remembered at different points that he had met Parmalee “more than thirty years earlier” or “in Osaka some forty years ago.” If the place was Osaka, the date was probably 1892-93, while Uchimura was teaching there. During this period, the trustees of the school that had employed him let the school go bankrupt, so it had to be bailed out by American missionaries. At the same time, Uchimura was working on How I Became a Christian. A few months later he reported that its “unpleasant observations about missionaries ... do not of course please them at all.” These conditions fit the specifics that he levelled against Parmalee that at the darkest period of his life she had “had no part whatever in all my struggles.” Despite all these painful associations etched in his memory, she did not even remember him. In addition, she wrote to him, “now a man sixty-seven years old, as if I were a boy of teens.” If my assumptions about their earlier meeting are correct, it would have been when Uchimura was in his early thirties and she was in her mid-forties.

This comparison of letters separated by more than seven decades from the controversy brings one to the following conclusions. When they first met, the struggling author felt that the American missionary woman had treated him with undeserved condescension. Uchimura’s subsequent outbursts against the superannuated Parmalee reflected his earlier contact with her in addition to his continuing exasperation with domineering women and the nonchalance with which missionaries so often treated converts. The exchange of correspondence subsided, but its effects continued. The following issue of the Japan Christian Intelligencer contained an announcement that the magazine would cease publication with the end of volume two the following month. The announcement gave as the only reason Uchimura’s desire “to concentrate our energy on the older and larger Seisho no Kenkyû.” The last issue quietly closed with an index for volume two that added a sense of determined finality. The Intelligencer went to sleep in the archives.

The frantic correspondence with Parmalee was the straw that broke the camel’s back. The circulation was down, but it was respectable given the audience Uchimura addressed. There appears to have been financial assistance and plenty of editorial copy, and the unchanged physical format implies continuing editorial assistance. One concludes that Uchimura felt the rewards did not repay the efforts.

Ota Yuzo concludes that the Japan Christian Intelligencer failed to achieve Uchimura’s stated aims when the magazine began: to proclaim true Christiantiy to Westerners and, in a broader sense, to work on their behalf. Ota judges that Uchimura failed on both counts. It was “impossible” to “open the eyes” of Westerners to Uchimura’s version of “true Christianity,” just as Westerners who showed so little understanding of and sympathy for Japanese failed in their evangelism. Written from an increasingly antiforeign perspective, the Intelligencer may have benefited Japanese Americans who could not read Uchimura’s Japanese and so fostered criticism of the United States among Japanese, but it did not meet his own desire to work on behalf of foreigners. These conclusions by Ota reflect a number of more specific points.

He takes Uchimura to task for the tone of his criticism. It accomplished nothing positive but simply “called up irrational racial sentiments.” As a result, his articles specifically worsened rather than improved relations, abetting the irrational nationalism that would dominate the 1930s. One certainly cannot deny this claim, but it ignores an important fact of the world in which Japanese internationalists acted. They could not know the “awful consequence” – to borrow Uchimura’s phrase from How I Became a Christian – of their acts. Their words reflected the new Japanese self-confidence after the First World War. Scholars in later generations know that the Taishô democrats, like liberals in Germany during the same period, made choices based on love for their country and a desire to see it respected that in a few years seemed to justify the most gross injustices. Specialists in Japanese-American relations such as Takagi Yasaka recognized the problem. Others, more convinced of Japan’s rectitude, revelled in Uchimura’s hyperbole as they ignored its dangers.

Although Ota’s comments correctly identify one of the chief blind spots in the worldview of Uchimura and his colleagues, his emphasis here on the unforeseen results of rhetoric like Uchimura’s does not greatly help in our attempt to evaluate the Japan Christian Intelligencer in terms of Uchimura’s own surroundings. Rather, it seems fair to conclude that, for all its faults, the Intelligencer occupies a worthy place in the history of Japan’s attempt to explain itself to Westerners and that in it Uchimura and his colleagues demonstrated a high level of competence as English-language journalists. At the same time, one adds that, in their dedication to the truth as they saw it, Uchimura’s deshi and in particular Uchimura himself so far overstepped the bounds of polite discourse as to lose all but their most patient readers. Perhaps the most difficult task for the student of a foreign language is to master nuances of persuasive criticism. In this, at least as many of their potential readers felt, the editors of the Intelligencer failed.

At this point, it is necessary to return to another section of Ota’s remarks to understand better the Japan Christian Intelligencer in terms of Uchimura’s development. In his discussion of Uchimura’s attacks on Parmalee as his “most hateful facet” and his agreement with Takeda Kiyoko that Uchimura’s reaction to Parmalee’s letter was almost “pathological,” Ota intimates that blind emotion increasingly affected Uchimura’s works. Certainly, Uchimura ranted at Parmalee in a manner inconsistent with his background either as a samurai or as a Christian gentleman. His hyperbole seemed to reflect more the strains imposed by Uchimura’s interpretation of Christianity and Kanzô’s reaction to criticism.

To examine the second point first, it was Parmalee’s misfortune to be an American woman. Uchimura responded to her criticism with all the stereotypes of his Western-educated colleagues as they lamented the unfeminine nature of Western professional women. The single-lady missionaries represented the cutting edge of the Western feminist movement of their day. Thus, what to Parmalee seemed “a decent courteous letter” elicited from Uchimura invective that Kanzô might have felt but never could have articulated in the face of strong-willed women. One senses that behind and yet through the pen of this accomplished old man Kanzô was relieving himself of his pent-up bile against his fretful mother, his frolicsom first wife, and in particular the officers of the lady missionary societies in the Connecticut Valley almost five decades earlier. In this sense, one can characterize these intemperate reactions as pathological, but to dismiss them as that alone does not locate them in their rightful setting.

Parmalee had started it all innocently enough. In her first letter to the intermediary Kimura Seimatsu, she defended her statement that Uchimura was making a new sect with words that deserve full quotation in the light of what happened later. “It is in just this way that new sects have started in the past. He may not give his followers a new name, but after he is dead some one may start up and say ‘we are Uchimuraites.’ I have frequently heard references to the Uchimura Kanzô church. But I do not suppose he himself in the least intends to start a new sect: but he may be doing it unconsciously all the same even while he denounces sects.”

No one knows if Kimura transmitted Parmalee’s amplification of her ideas to Uchimura. If they were included in the general remarks that he sent, they would have reached Uchimura a few days after he had made the statements about Parmalee before 700 of his followers. His diary for that day shows he had been thinking about her comments on the church when he spoke: “Tsukamoto talked about the problem of the church based on Matthew 16:16-18. It was most enjoyable. By way of introduction, I outlined my opposition to the opinion of an American missionary on this problem which had been addressed to me.” In the next issue of the Japan Christian Intelligencer, on 10 December, he published an English version of the above lecture by Tsukamoto. Uchimura specifically called it his “reply to Miss H. Frances Parmalee ... who severely criticized me and my article on Sectarianism.” The text of the article contains Jesus’ reference to the apostle Peter as the “rock” that forms the basis of the Roman Catholic Church’s claim of direct apostolic succession. It is perhaps the best text to discuss when one tries to link notions of God to the church or churches of the world.

Tsukamoto used the text to develop an answer consistent with Uchimura’s idea of the church. “I would rather remain a ‘church-less’ Christian than be a member of a ‘Christless’ Church ... The Christian Church must stand upon the living faith in Christ. The ‘living stone, chosen of God, and precious’ must be her bedrock (I Peter 2:4).” By shifting the textual basis to I Peter, Tsukamoto identified the “Lord” as the “living stone” and the individual believers as “living stones” that build up a “spiritual house.” This interpretation continued the metaphor but changed the nature of Jesus’ legacy to include believers not affiliated with an established church. Tsukamoto clearly abridged Uchimura’s position, but it was not to be expanded or refined, since the same issue that contained it announced the discontinuation of the Japan Christian Intelligencer. Parmalee did not want to debate, and Uchimura, without dialogue, could hardly say more.

Here one understands why in this exchange with Parmalee Uchimura became almost “pathological.” A dislike of domineering women and a demand for correct forms of respect could provoke similar outbursts in numerous people well into their seventh decade. In this case, these very human needs were abetted by another: the hope of an aging leader that his work would be continued. Parmalee’s questioning of his motive – that he might subconsciously want to found a church – struck a sensitive nerve. In using the article of a young follower as a statement of his own position, Uchimura also tacitly acknowledged his own age. In his diary entry describing the mailing of the last issue of the Japan Christian Intelligencer, he speculated that by “ending the smaller magazine” he was “practicing to provide a good end for the larger magazine.”

Tsukamoto Toraji, whose words about the church Uchimura had owned to be his own, appeared in both magazines. As Uchimura’s closest colleague, he had reason to believe that he would take up Uchimura’s endeavours when the sensei stepped down. Uchimura was attracted by the prospect, and from that matrix of attitudes developed the final drama of Uchimura’s life. It involved the deshi, and a survey of these followers closest to Uchimura in his final decade precedes discussion of the ensuing tragedy.
zh: 對日本外交關係的關切幫助塑造了內村的生涯，除了他從《萬朝報》退休到參與再臨運動這段時期外，它始終是他的主要興趣。作為《萬朝報》的外交事務專家，內村曾向讀者推薦西方的做法。當他再次把目光投向日本以外的世界時，日本人的自我認知已經發生了很大變化。他們更加自信了，不再認為凡是西方的就因此更好。內村表示同意；他周圍所看到的似乎在某種程度上實現了他早年的夢想。他鼓勵弟子去幫助其他國家的貧困者。他擁有更廣泛的海外友人圈。而且他作為自己民族的代表，開始譴責那些似乎貶低日本的他人的態度和行為。最初，對英語的有力運用令他精神振奮，但後來卻使他逐漸衰弱，因為他發現即使他的流利英語也無法贏得外國人的認可。
討論首先說明內村的日本同胞如何理解「外國人」這個詞。他們將世界分為「內」與「外」兩個範疇，外國一詞特指西歐與美國的代表。這些人也容易被籠統地稱為「白人」，不過通常他們用一個通俗用語「外人」——「來自國境之外的人」——來指稱。世界其他地區的民族雖然以其所在地名稱呼，卻不被列入外人的範疇。

當日本人看出這種差異並將其表現為種族問題時，「白人」對「有色人種」，這種差異如同鑑三的童年時期一樣，持續反映出經濟地位的不同。白種人民似乎無限地更加富裕。內村記得他早年與這些人痛苦的接觸經驗。當他從留學歸來時，他迴避外國人，儘管他在《萬朝報》的職位要求他向外國人闡述日本的觀點。離開那份工作後，他們在很大程度上從他的心裡淡去了。他很少與他們相遇，當他相遇時，他的接觸就像他那些受過良好教育的同儕一樣，基本上是被動的。西方思想家的著作激勵了他，但他將英文寫作限制於個人通信，以及自一九一三年起，在每月《聖書之研究》首頁上的單段冥想。

內村生涯最後的十年中，重新與西方人士有了更廣泛的接觸。他似乎是個國際主義者，與其他受過外交訓練的日本人相似，然而，如下文所示，有幾項特質將他與眾不同：他對西方人的理解之深、接觸面之廣，以及他對非洲人和亞洲同胞福祉的關切。很少有日本人明白，那些令他在與西方人往來時感到不快的經濟落差和缺乏尊重的因素，同樣也影響著日後所謂第三世界的人民。他深知日本有義務反抗西方人的優越感假設，並幫助那些更不幸的人。他將兄弟般的接觸和傳教事業視為基督教信仰的一部分而予以推動。他很少察覺自己幫助他人的願望與對待持同樣動機來自他方的人所採取的冷淡態度之間的矛盾，但他確保他的團體提供的援助是通過展現基督教慈悲的個人傳達給受助者的。對這些對不幸民族的反應的討論，引入了對西方人際關係更深入的考察。
內村及其門徒與日本幾乎所有其他新教徒一樣，都認為傳福音是信仰的迫切要求。他們組織學生團體在夏季將信仰傳入鄉間，並成立宣教會社募集經費用於中國和非洲的工作。

一九二二年，一場臨時性會議建立了一個宣教社。其後兩期的《聖書之研究》刊登了四頁的佈道增刊，隨後的社員大會募集捐獻。內村建議他們在中國開展工作，因為他認為日本與中國在種族與文化上是一體的。儘管有這樣的接近性，他繼續說，日本精神將日本人與中國人區分開來，反而使日本人更接近英國與美國。然而這兩個國家卻派出自我犧牲的宣教士前往中國。作為開始，內村建議捐獻給中華內地會。這個英國組織因在中國進行的實踐性鄉村工作而享有聲譽，且與中國同工保持密切合作，這種服事方式正是內村所嚮往的。他所在團體的款項被送給了一位鄉村醫生。這位英國籍醫療宣教士寄來的定期通信詳述了他如何用這筆款項雇用中國醫生協助他的工作。

在法屬赤道非洲的宣教士協會工作，源於祐之在德國建立的聯繫。他在那裡認識了阿爾貝特‧施韋澤，這位德國管風琴家‧神學家‧哲學家‧醫生‧佈道家。施韋澤放棄了在德國燦爛的職業生涯，在非洲創辦了一所宣教醫院。到了一九二○年代，全世界的基督徒都認識他，把他視為基督教救濟貧困者之責任的主要體現者之一。祐之發現施韋澤讀過《我如何成為基督徒》，並欽佩他父親的工作，因而感到榮幸。通過祐之的引薦，兩位年長的人士互相通信。內村的宣教士協會為施韋澤的工作做出了貢獻。這種聯繫在第二次世界大戰後得以延續，當時受內村影響的日本醫生在非洲服事。

雖然這項工作使內村團體的注意力轉向世界其他地區的關切，但他與朝鮮人的接觸卻讓他熟悉了其他亞洲人，儘管嚴格來說朝鮮人並非外國人。日本在一九一○年併吞了朝鮮，但日本人並不認為朝鮮人是兄弟。一個官僚性的日本精英階層統治朝鮮。偶有朝鮮人擔任下級職位，但他們毫無實權。一九一九年，朝鮮人驚人的消極抵抗示威向日本人警示了他們實際控制力之薄弱。日本人對示威者的野蠻攻擊加上象徵性的和解姿態，只是進一步激化了朝鮮人的敵意。
內村是為數甚少的日本人之一，他理解朝鮮人的願望並同情他們。他在日記中頻繁提及他們。不少朝鮮人訂閱《聖書之研究》，其中幾位在返鄉前曾參加過內村的聖經講座。內村的著作已被譯成朝鮮文，在當地內村仍被尊為聖經權威。

這份友好關係早就開始了。內村與朝鮮人合作順暢有效，因為他尊重他們，也因此得到尊重。他寫信給貝爾說：「我們之間沒有『種族問題』。從那些傲慢無情的美國和英國宣教士對待我的方式，我多少知道應該怎樣對待所謂的『低等』民族。」在對一群朝鮮青年的講演中，內村強調了人類本質上的兄弟情誼，這來自於為了共同目標（如基督教佈道）而進行的共同工作。《聖書之研究》的一位朝鮮訂閱者述說他已讀遍內村的著作「六次」，而當他意識到內村是日本人時，「敵對的日本變得溫和而可愛了」。我不知道還有其他日朝之間這樣的相互好感。根據這份經驗，內村不滿其政府的政策也就不足為奇了。他相信「可憐的朝鮮人失去了他們的國家，沒有什麼能夠安慰他們的喪失……日本吞併朝鮮如同吞了一個波蘭，她絕不可能完全消化這一口」。他尊重朝鮮人深刻的信仰和愛國心。當他在講演中提到民族主義時，「那些聽得手心出汗的正是來自朝鮮的學生」。其中一位聽講如此專注的學生返回祖國，後來成為了「朝鮮的甘地」。
朝鮮的殖民地統治者並不歡迎內村的訪問。他的朋友曾邀請他前往，但他從日本政府的關係人士那裡得知自己不受歡迎。這再好不過地證明了他對朝鮮人的影響力，以及他們對他的尊重。在內村和他最開明的同僚看來，中國和朝鮮，就像非洲一樣，是日本人應當表達基督教手足之情的地區。日本有經濟力量，至少有些日本人感受到了提供這種援助的責任。
但朝鮮並非唯一吸引人們關注的亞洲地區。東印度詩人兼哲學家泰戈爾和民族精神領袖甘地在日本成為家喻戶曉的人物。他們所代表的印度並未喚起慈善心，反而贏得了人們對這一古老傳統的敬重——這一傳統既容納西方影響，卻又不受其束縛。

內村把泰戈爾列入「新思想家」之列，同時還包括哲學家魯道夫‧歐根、亨利‧柏格森和伯特蘭‧羅素。在一次聖誕節講談中談及三博士來朝的預言時，他提及某些西方人的預言——亞洲人能比西方人更好地詮釋基督教。他指出，當這些人說起「亞洲人」時，他們未必是指「日本人」。「像泰戈爾這樣的人才是真正代表性的亞洲人。誰能說泰戈爾所代表的精神不能最好地詮釋基督呢？」泰戈爾在一九一六年和一九二四年間在日本進行的講演中談論過一個「浸潤於印度精神傳統」的「亞洲」。內村沒有提及這些訪問。可以推測，與其他日本知識領袖一樣，他本會不贊成泰戈爾對印度價值的強調。

對於甘地，內村表達了毫無保留的敬重，認為他代表了對人類尊嚴的訴求，比泰戈爾的表達更為直接。甘地的非暴力主義尤其吸引了他。內村讀到甘地遭判入獄六年，甘地卻回應說獲釋後將繼續進行非暴力抵抗。內村由此得出結論：甘地就這樣用基督教的方法對抗一個自稱基督教的強權！他的非暴力主義所表現的高尚情操，超越了克倫威爾和彌爾頓的黨派之心與暴力行為。內村祈禱日本人能效法甘地的行動，為亞洲獨立奠定堅實基礎，但他懷疑日本能否產生出像甘地這樣的人物——甘地「似乎是被上帝派來作亞洲拯救者的」。
在泰戈爾與甘地身上，內村聽到了自己的聲音。他們自豪地稱自己是「亞洲人」，接納西方的標準，將之化為己有，然後主張與西方人平等，甚或超越他們。憑藉這些本領，甘地將拯救亞洲。沒有朝鮮人能像甘地對英國人那樣與日本統治者對話，但內村也許可以寄望於——特別是從自己的朝鮮信徒中——會有這樣一個人，受甘地啟發，挺身而出。

幫助他人的願望和對亞洲人的歡迎，都容易被納入日本獨特的「使命」這一框架之下。內村思考日本在世界歷史上的使命已經有三十年了，但到了一九二○年代中期，許多其他日本人也開始關切這一問題。人們難以衡量西方殖民統治的受害者在各地之間所結成的情感紐帶，但十年後，當日本將領尋求支持、用亞洲兄弟情誼和「亞洲人的亞洲」之類溫和的說辭來包裝其意圖時，這種情感就派上了用場。本論述迄今探討的是內村對某些外國人的態度，但並非指外人（gaijin），即一九四五年之前日本人認為唯一重要的外國人。這些西歐人和北美人主導著日本人對外部世界的關注。這一執念貫穿於下面對內村態度的詳細考察中。
在他人生的最後十年，內村延續並加強了早年的既有模式。他與外國人保持著定期的通信往來，但儘管有這些接觸，他與其他受過教育的日本人一樣，對西方人作為一個整體感到不信任。他的厭惡感是有根據的。西方人不能欣賞日本人禮儀談吐的精妙之處，也不能認可日本人民的成就。內村創辦了一份英文雜誌，試圖向他們介紹日本的美德。經過兩年的努力後，他決定把「餘下的精力」投注到他的日文雜誌上。這些話題中的每一個都值得深入探討。

一九二○年代初期，內村喪失了最後一位把他引入信仰的外國友人。哈里斯主教去世了。內村與哈里斯始終保持親密的往來，儘管哈里斯在一九○四至一九一六年間先後被任命為日本及朝鮮的主教，這使他幾乎沒有閒暇時間。哈里斯作為主教的種種身分標識本會令內村厭惡，因為他對任何形式的教會權威都很反感。但在哈里斯於一九一六年退休後，內村的態度改變了。此時哈里斯已成為名人。德富蘇峰為英文版首爾報紙報導了哈里斯在朝鮮的退休。他寫道，哈里斯的「六英尺高的男子漢身軀、銀髮蓋頂、心中充滿天堂的歡樂與對人的愛、面容如晨曦般明亮、既不懼魔鬼亦不懼世界、沉著篤定的步履，這一切都說明了他是何等樣的人物。」

哈里斯獲得了官方日本的認可，其恢宏的氣度也相稱。1898年的一項皇室勳章表彰了他在加州對日本人的工作。退休那年的另一項勳章無疑反映了官方的認可——他作為主教，曾讚許日本對朝鮮的統治。幾年後，據說他獲得的皇室勳章超過了任何其他外國人。內村並未在公開場合與他的老師在這些看法上表示不同意，儘管他通常較為保留的朋友、長老會領袖植村正久確實曾以簡短的評論批評哈里斯，認為日本人不需要那些如此錯誤地讚美自己國家的朋友。
這位退休主教與那位十年前曾與內村一起哀悼哈里斯夫人去世的鰥夫判若兩人。如今哈里斯再度成為恩人的身分，他曾在《基督徒的安慰》出版後不久告訴這位年輕作者，他是多麼享受閱讀這部著作。正因為他們長期以來的相互欣賞，內村在1917年那個灰暗的日子裡，當他尋求有人介紹他演講路德時，便轉向了這位仁兄。而哈里斯本人也樂於自豪地把內村介紹給輕井澤的宣教士們，並在自己位於東京的家中享受他的蒞臨。
一九二一年一月，哈里斯出席了內村關於《羅馬書》的一次講座，並親自簡短地談及自己雖已近八十高齡，仍有意重返講壇的打算。但這終未成事。哈里斯於四月患病，次月去世。內村在訃告中稱讚這對哈里斯夫婦：「他們影響我，不是藉著教義或教會權威，而是藉著愛與信任。」幾天後，內村臥病在床，患上「眩暈、發顫和噁心」。在他自己精神發展中最後的中介者已經離世，內村感到了歲月的沉重。

內村長久以來的美國朋友中，還有兩位來訪。精神科醫生馬丁‧巴爾（Martin Barr）是內村在賓州艾爾文時期的舊友，於四月抵達，在為期近四個月的逗留期間參觀了精神疾病護理機構。七月間，大衛‧貝爾（David C. Bell）偕子來訪，停留九日。內村把他們介紹給弟子們，並與他們長時間敘舊。三位客人搭乘同一艘船返鄉，內村為多年通信所保持的溫情而歎為觀止。在哈里斯及其他美國人身上，他體驗到了一種任何年齡都難得一見、且與他對大多數外國人的態度大相逕庭的深厚友誼。

與他親密的美國朋友形成鮮明對比，內村對英國人感到最少的同情。一九二二年，他在寫給貝爾的信中說，他唯一的英國朋友是J‧W‧羅伯遜-斯科特，我們已經看到內村曾將他帶到一位鄉村地主的家中。羅伯遜-斯科特創辦了《鄉村人》雜誌，旨在面向地主階層和那些嚮往優雅鄉村生活的人士。他對鄉村生活的興趣促使他在第一次世界大戰期間來到日本，他歸國後出版的《日本的基礎》一書，在四十年後隆納德‧多爾發表關於土地改革的著作前，一直是瞭解日本鄉村最好的資料來源。
當羅勃遜-史考特的介紹會安排到內村時，兩人迅速成為朋友。他們一起旅遊的機會讓內村得以向羅勃遜-史考特傾訴，日本強制現代化對耕作辛苦、腳踏實地的農民造成了嚴重傷害。羅勃遜-史考特訪問歸來，用一個向日本朋友借來的描述來總結他對內村的感受：「日本的卡萊爾」和「以色列的擾亂者」。內村則把他的朋友視為「開放的理性主義者，一個堅強、誠實的人」。
如果說內村感到缺少許多盎格魯‧撒克遜的朋友，他在北歐卻有許多朋友。《我如何成為基督徒》的譯本使他獲得了關心宗教的知識人的認可。他與許多人通信往來，像勇四這樣的日本學生因為他父親的名聲而受到熱烈歡迎。
內村欠下這許多聯繫的人情於威廉‧貢德特，他那部《我如何成為基督徒》的原始譯本銷售量達四到五萬冊，並引發了其他譯本的問世。儘管兩人不再一起工作，內村一家和貢德特一家仍保持友誼，內村在一九二〇年向他的弟子提及，他和家人曾蒙貢德特告知"德國人民美好的一面"。

貢德特曾將一位來自圖賓根的教授帶到內村的一場聚會，並將來客的談話流暢地譯成日語。內村在歐洲的弟子寄來的信件透露了那邊完全出人意料的支持。其中一人從巴黎寫信說，他曾將《日本之代表人物》的副本贈予索邦大學校長，校長稱讚它為著名的經典著作，也贈予政治家克里蒙梭，據聞克里蒙梭表示，如果身體允許，他願意赴日本會見作者。又有一天，郵差送來一封信，是艾伯特‧史懷哲的出版商寄來的。他讀過內村的《獨與上帝與我》——一部英文冥想集——讀後感覺「如同聆聽巴赫的音樂」。
內村的著作雖然使他與當代最富活力的歐洲學者有所接觸，但身邊的宣教士們卻不斷提醒他，並非所有外國人都是超人。作為一個整體，宣教士們似乎注定——幾乎與其說是因為他們本身的所作所為，毋寧說是因為內村棘手的性格——與內村發生令人不快的衝突。他始終批判性十足，很快就能從他們的言辭中推斷出居高臨下的態度。
宣教士和他的追隨者認為內村在某種意義上是「反宣教士的」。事實上，迄今為止許多相關的論述表明，他的反應並非簡單劃一。他接受宣教士邀請在他們家中投宿。他們的好客品質使他們成為日本牧師間所謂的「好宣教士」——那些遵循社交往來常規、志業相同的人。不是「好宣教士」的人並不被稱為「壞宣教士」。「壞宣教士」才是刻板印象的基礎。觀察這些預設觀念，可以反映他與宣教士的關係在內村年邁後的具體性質。

他對宣教士提出的普遍指控建立在三個要點上：他們不尊重我們或我們的文化；他們不學我們的語言；他們將教會和實利置於信仰之上。因為宣教士不尊重我們的文化，他們把我們全都看作我們當中最輕浮的少數人。在一場主日講座之後，聽眾中的一位成員要求與內村約談，並請求金錢。這一舉動毀了內村這一整天的心情。「我想像著有人等待著一位宣教士從講台上走下來，然後向這位宣教士懇求金錢。這讓我感到難受，」大概是因為那位宣教士會因此得出結論，認為所有日本人都在向輕信的外國人討要施捨。當一位宣教士拜訪內村並問他依靠誰時，內村說：「上帝、我自己，以及我的同胞。」那位宣教士問起這樣的信仰如何能在東方人身上發展，語氣中顯然帶有懷疑，彷彿認為任何歸信者若沒有宣教士的協助便無法傳福音。內村認為，這樣的評論表明了對日本文化的無知。
他認為，宣教士對於日語工作投入甚少，正足以說明這種無知。在他一篇題為《宣教士與語言》的簡短英文冥想文中，他簡潔地指出
> 我們知道有英國和美國宣教士在日本居住了二十年、三十年，甚至四十年，卻仍然說不出像樣的日語……至於宣教士的閱讀能力，簡直可以忽略不計。百人中沒有一個能讀懂通俗報紙，我們根本不知道有誰能讀懂原文的普通日本文學。難怪他們無法理解我們，在這個國家裡度過了半生之後，仍然對我們一無所知。這些宣教士輕視我們的語言這一事實，清楚地證明了他們對我們的靈魂根本沒有真實的愛。
他的最後這一點源於前兩點：那些對日本人幾乎毫無同情心的個人，把自己教派的擴張置於信仰本身之上。保羅曾試圖縮小自己與他人之間的文化差異，但來日本的宣教士卻不同。他們甚至要求我們改變宗教、放棄習俗、與親人對抗：然而他們自己卻無法改變他們的教派。而他們按歸信者的數量來評估自己的工作。
這些素描雖然可能有所誇大，但其他方面都有根據，這一點由內村在一九二六年夏季的活動所證明。內村在東京西邊群山中輪王澤西方數英里處租了一棟日式房舍。他曾在一九一八年在那裡進行過非常成功的講演。輪王澤是由宣教士社群成員開發為避暑勝地的。在夏季的幾個月內，它大概是日本最具國際色彩的社區。他的日記告訴我們，在這段時期內，內村前往輪王澤五次，藉以緩解他那充滿持續不斷的閱讀和寫作的「度假」生活。
有一次，他去探訪老朋友漢娜‧瑞德爾（Hannah Riddell，1855–1932），一位聖公會宣教士，內村稱她為「謙卑而聰慧的女性」，是日本二十萬名痲瘋病患的「母親」。他感謝上帝讓他能對她的事工有所貢獻。瑞德爾小姐「效法了南丁格爾的榜樣」。她從一八九五年開始在九州痲瘋病患中展開的工作「在日本社會福利的史冊中為她贏得了永久的地位」。
三天後，應加拿大衛理公會宣教士丹尼爾‧諾曼（1864-1941，歷史學家赫伯特‧諾曼之父）的邀請，內村在輕井澤的「日本人教會」發表演講。他向兩百多名聽眾講述了克拉克的故事，並得出結論：政府聘用的平信徒外國人比宣教士更出色的傳教者。即使宣教士離開日本，基督教仍將繁榮昌盛。內村後來在日記中寫道，他為自己說過那番話感到後悔——雖然是受宣教士邀請發言，但他認為自己必須如實描述情況。
後來他租了計程車，帶著家人遊覽輕井澤的風景名勝。輕井澤被稱為「宣教士和東京人的夏季首都」，他的結論是「看一次就足夠了」。不到一週後，為悼念關東大地震三週年而舉行的追悼會又把他帶回輕井澤。在那裡，一位英國宣教士在街上的舉止激怒了他，那位宣教士把他「當作小孩對待……我們日本信徒應該合作，盡快把這樣的宣教士趕出去。只要他們還在這裡，基督的聖名就只會被褻瀆。」

一週後，美國人梅瑞爾‧沃里斯邀請內村到他家中做客。二十世紀初，沃里斯原本在美國從事建築設計工作，但醫生診斷他患肺結核只能活一年，於是他放棄執業來到日本傳教。在日本他的健康得以恢復，娶了一位日本女性為妻，開設了建築設計事務所，並利用美國藥膏薄荷油與哈蒙德風琴在日本銷售所得的利潤，創辦了一個基督教互助組織。內村讚揚沃里斯的事業，敦促讀者銘記確實存在著這樣的美國人。在內村去世後三十多年，沃里斯迅速公開了內村與他往來的信件，以答覆有關他們相互關係的疑問。
當他拜訪沃里斯時，內村聽說許多外國人正在拋棄基督教而改信佛教，因此日本人必須向外國人闡揚基督教的原則，正如他在數月前所言。既然如此，「我無法理解那些宣教士的用意，他們試圖向我們教導基督教，卻沒有認識到它在他們的故鄉已經衰落。」

這五次短暫的輕井澤之行，展現了內村試圖與宣教士合作所面臨的各種問題。許多史料證實漢娜‧里德爾、梅瑞爾‧沃里斯和丹尼爾‧諾曼都是「優秀的」宣教士。然而輕井澤度假地卻有著分別為西方人和日本人設置的教堂。諾曼舉行聚會的「日本人教堂」不禁令人懷疑那些動聽的基督教弟兄姊妹情誼。內村本人則感到不安，因為他說著自己認為宣教士們不樂於聽聞的話語。而街上那位英國宣教士，無論他做什麼或說什麼，都未能消解那些老一套的刻板印象。

對於宣教士及其角色的困惑，如這些例子所反映的那樣，扭曲了內村的晚年生活。內村對宣教士為何來日本知之甚少。他們以回應自己認為是上帝所定的命令而自願在世界的遙遠角落服事。直到一個世紀後，新教宣教運動的起源和動力才開始獲得歷史學家應有的關注。除了他們應當奉上帝之名進行佈道的信念外，宣教士還尋求冒險。在沒有電影、廣播、電視、電郵或互聯網提供資訊的時代，他們向支持者介紹異域風情。在他們所謂的「海外禾場」，他們勞碌而寂寞。輕井澤這樣的夏日避暑勝地為他們的孩子提供了一種類似於「故鄉」——他們父母來自的國家——那樣的生活氣息。有些宣教士以略帶嘲諷的口吻說，宣教士就像糞肥一樣：分散開來時有益，聚在一起時則臭烘烘的。使「輕井澤的社會氛圍……對內村一點也不融洽」的原因，一部分來自這種異常密集的現象——而這正是在他眼中貶低宣教事工的因素。

宣教士與他們赴任地區專業同僚之間的關係，需要進一步的研究。這樣的研究也應該能夠照亮後來政府派遣的技術顧問對較不發達國家所做的宣教努力。內村所言為一位敏銳而自尊的人提供了雄辯的見證——此人畢生致力於為自己國家的美德爭取認可——但這只是故事的一個層面，而且是很少被如此清楚表達的層面。內村造訪輕井澤時心中所思所想的一部分，源自於他前兩年所從事的兩項事業。一九二四年，他加入了日本運動，對新的美國移民法進行了激烈抗議，該法禁止亞洲人移民。隨後在一九二六年初，他創辦了一份英文雜誌，宣教士成為其既定讀者的重要組成部分。這兩項事業塑造了他對外國人的最終態度。

一九二四年的《移民法案》反映了美國對日本態度的改變，並在日本本身引發了惶恐。自從二十年前日本在對俄戰爭中取得決定性勝利以來，日本在西方一直享有崇高的地位。日本在第一次世界大戰期間向中國提出的《二十一條要求》以及幾年後對俄羅斯的軍事干預，消耗殆盡了這份善意。對移民勞動力的反對使日本成為美國西岸政治中的國內問題。來自世界其他地區的移民造成了需要立即採取行動的問題。加爾文‧柯立芝總統心中有比日本更多的事要考慮，他思量著包括禁止亞洲所有地區移民的法案。

日本人把問題看得更為簡單。他們想知道自己是否還能保持因快速現代化而從西方人那裡獲得的優遇地位。日本在國際聯盟中的高地位證實了這一特殊角色。日本領導人曾任命內村鑑三的至交新渡戶稻造為聯盟副秘書長；作為副秘書長，新渡戶是聯盟內圈唯一的非歐洲人。在他退休後的七十多年裡，才又有另一位日本人在國際組織中獲得類似的高位。新渡戶在日內瓦的倡議將帶來深遠的後果。當時沒人能預測到。相反，日本人堅持期盼美國總統柯立芝會在議案在國會委員會和議院中曲折前行後予以否決。經過長時間思量可能的後果後，柯立芝簽署了該法案，從而打碎了日本人的希望。內村鑑三寫道，他的舉動可能預示著「日本的滅亡」。
